doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Piano duos, Mingus and the seventies
title: The Half Note and its move uptown
summary: They describe the odd room, the family atmosphere and its failed move to West Fifty-Fourth.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: The Half Note was a strange . . . it was a wonderful club but it was a strange set up.
For those of you who weren’t there do you want to tell them what the set up was like?

[A] small club with a bandstand . . . a high bandstand with a bar in front of it and kind of a room in back of it for tables. As I remember when Coltrane played there they didn’t come off the stand during the intermission. They just sat there. Probably handed up whatever they were handed. It was a very family kind of affair there with the parents cooking meatballs and things like that. Going downstairs to the basement to get high. With Lennie we usually finished a set and he grabbed one of our arms and we walked out to someone’s car and the club was filled with his students and they’d say, “Okay what are we going to expect next?” Things like that. Very strange.

Yes. I remember after they closed that place at Spring and Hudson and they moved it uptown, which was a bomb. It only lasted a year or two. It turned into a place they called “The Only-Est Place”. Do you remember that? Because I
remember hearing you there which just a bass. It might’ve been with Harvey Schwartz and maybe Jeff Williams. I don’t remember exactly.
This was after the life of the Half Note up there?

Yeah. Somebody bought it and renamed it “The Only-Est Place”. I remember I met Ron Odrich that night. He came and sat in with you on bass clarinet. But the place tanked shortly thereafter. I didn’t last long which is too bad. If the Cantarinos had bought that building and kept it they probably still would be there. They made a big mistake by moving uptown because as you know . . .
Oh, if they bought the old building, you mean?
Yeah. If they bought the old building, which now is gone, which now is a Korean deli.
Yeah, oh God, it’s weird. They were offered to buy?

I’m told they had an offer to buy that building and turned it down and somebody talked them into moving up to West Fifty-Fourth instead and they went up there and you know what happened with that place.
Only a couple years. The whole vibe of the old place was gone. It was really expensive as they were doing double bills.
But for a while I thought they were doing okay.
